options.why: Step scaling is still reactive, so instances arrive 7 minutes after the climb begins.

options.text: Add a predictive scaling policy.
options.why: Predictive scaling learns the recurring pattern from history and launches capacity ahead of forecast peaks, adapting as the pattern drifts.

questions.explain: Reactive scaling cannot beat slow instance launch. For recurring patterns, predictive scaling forecasts and launches in advance; scheduled scaling is for known one-off or fixed events. Warm pools shorten launch time.

questions.stem: A retailer publishes order and return events from several services. The data team wants to start a new fraud-scoring consumer next month and must feed it the last 30 days of events first, without asking producers to resend anything. Routing should stay rule-based so new consumers can be added without changing the producers. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Send the events to an Amazon EventBridge event bus with an archive that retains 30 days, and replay the archive to the new consumer's rule.
options.why: EventBridge archives keep events for a set period and can replay them to rules, while rules route events by content.

options.text: Publish the events to an Amazon SNS standard topic with an SQS queue per consumer.
options.why: Fan-out works for future events, but a standard topic keeps no history to replay to a consumer that subscribes later.

options.text: Send the events to a single SQS queue with a 14-day message retention period.
options.why: Messages go to one consumer and are deleted after processing; the maximum retention of 14 days is also short of 30.

options.text: Have each producer also write its events to a DynamoDB table for the new consumer to scan.
options.why: It changes every producer and leaves the team to build its own replay and routing.

questions.explain: When the requirement includes 'replay past events' with rule-based routing, think EventBridge archive and replay (or a log such as Kinesis or MSK when throughput is very high). Queues delete messages once consumed.

questions.stem: An online pharmacy must keep backups of its order database (Amazon RDS) and its EBS volumes for 7 years. A ransomware tabletop exercise showed that an attacker with stolen administrator credentials could delete backups. The company needs backups that no one, including administrators and the root user, can delete before the retention period ends. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Copy all snapshots to a second account every night with a Lambda function that a separate team owns.
options.why: Separating accounts helps, but nothing makes the copies immutable, and the custom copy job is extra code to run.

options.text: Use AWS Backup with a backup vault that has AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode and a 7-year minimum retention.
options.why: Once the cooling-off period ends, compliance-mode Vault Lock cannot be changed or removed by anyone, so recovery points cannot be deleted early.

options.text: Use RDS automated backups with the maximum retention period and Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager policies for the EBS snapshots.
options.why: RDS automated backups keep at most 35 days, and administrators can delete DLM-managed snapshots.

options.text: Use AWS Backup with a vault access policy that denies backup:DeleteRecoveryPoint to all IAM principals.
options.why: An administrator can edit or remove the vault access policy, so this stops accidents but not a stolen admin credential.

questions.explain: Immutable backups on AWS: AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode (WORM for recovery points). Policies that deny deletes stop mistakes, not attackers who can rewrite the policy.

questions.stem: A retailer's CloudWatch Logs bill keeps growing because every log group from 300 services is set to 'Never expire'. Engineers only search the last 30 days, but compliance requires keeping all application logs for 1 year at the lowest possible cost, with retrieval in hours being acceptable. Which combination of actions meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Choose two.)

options.text: Stream the logs through a subscription filter to Amazon Data Firehose into S3, with a lifecycle rule that moves objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and expires them after 1 year.
options.why: S3 with a Glacier lifecycle is far cheaper for the year-long archive, and retrieval within hours is acceptable.

options.text: Keep 'Never expire' and use CloudWatch Logs Insights only for the last 30 days.
options.why: Query scope changes nothing about storage, so the bill keeps growing.

options.text: Set the retention of each log group to 1 year in CloudWatch Logs.
options.why: It meets compliance but keeps a year of logs in CloudWatch storage, which costs more than S3 archive classes.

options.text: Move the logs to an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain with 1 year of hot storage.
options.why: OpenSearch is great for search, but a year of hot storage is much more expensive than an archive.

options.text: Set the retention of each log group to 30 days.
options.why: CloudWatch Logs then deletes older events automatically, so the team stops paying CloudWatch storage for logs nobody searches.

questions.explain: Keep logs hot only as long as people query them, then archive to S3 with lifecycle rules. Log groups with 'Never expire' are a classic slow cost leak.

questions.stem: A fashion retailer's product detail pages run the same few hundred queries against an Aurora MySQL cluster thousands of times per second. The writer and two replicas are at 80% CPU, and product data changes only a few times per hour. The team needs sub-millisecond read latency for these queries. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Add three more Aurora Replicas to the cluster.
options.why: More replicas share the load, but each read is still a database query in milliseconds, and they cost more than a cache.

options.text: Enable Aurora Serverless v2 for the readers.
options.why: Serverless capacity scales the database but does not make repeated reads sub-millisecond.

options.text: Move the product data into Amazon S3 and query it with Athena.
options.why: Athena is for analytics, with query times in seconds, not for serving web pages.

options.text: Cache query results in ElastiCache with a TTL.
options.why: An in-memory cache returns repeated results in sub-millisecond time and removes most of the load from the database.

questions.explain: Read-heavy, rarely changing, repeated queries are the textbook case for caching. Add replicas when reads are diverse; add a cache when they repeat. Pick a TTL that matches how stale the data may be.

questions.stem: An order-management app runs on an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster with a single writer instance and connects through hundreds of short-lived Lambda invocations. During the last writer failure, the cluster took several minutes to recover and the functions saw a storm of connection errors. Which combination of actions will MOST reduce disruption during a future failure? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add an Aurora Replica in a different Availability Zone so it can be promoted to writer.
options.why: With a replica available, Aurora promotes it instead of recreating the writer, which is much faster.

options.text: Connect the functions through Amazon RDS Proxy.
options.why: RDS Proxy keeps a connection pool, holds client connections during failover, and routes to the new writer without waiting for DNS.

options.text: Move the cluster to a larger writer instance class.
options.why: More capacity does not change how long a failover takes when there is no replica to promote.

options.text: Create a cross-Region read replica of the cluster.
options.why: That is for Regional DR; promoting it is a much slower and broader operation than an in-Region failover.

options.text: Raise the Lambda function timeout to 15 minutes.
options.why: Functions would just wait longer and keep connections open, adding to the storm.

questions.explain: Aurora failover is fast when a replica exists to promote. RDS Proxy smooths it further for applications with many connections, especially Lambda, by pooling and redirecting without DNS lag.

questions.stem: A retailer's legacy loyalty-points database runs on an unencrypted Amazon RDS for MySQL DB instance. A new compliance rule requires encryption at rest with a KMS key, and a short maintenance window is acceptable. Which combination of steps will produce an encrypted database? (Choose three.)

options.text: Copy the snapshot and choose a KMS key so the copy is encrypted.
options.why: Copying a snapshot is the step where encryption can be added.

options.text: Restore a new DB instance from the encrypted snapshot copy and point the application at it.
options.why: A DB instance restored from an encrypted snapshot is encrypted at rest.

options.text: Modify the existing DB instance and turn on storage encryption.
options.why: RDS does not allow turning on encryption for an existing unencrypted DB instance.

options.text: Create an encrypted read replica of the unencrypted instance and promote it.
options.why: You cannot create an encrypted read replica from an unencrypted DB instance.

options.text: Set an encryption parameter in the DB parameter group and reboot the instance.
options.why: Storage encryption is not a parameter group setting.

options.text: Take a manual snapshot of the unencrypted DB instance.
options.why: The snapshot is the starting point; you cannot encrypt the running instance itself.

questions.explain: RDS encryption at rest is chosen when an instance is created. To encrypt an existing one: snapshot, copy the snapshot with a KMS key, then restore. The same pattern works for unencrypted EBS volumes.

questions.stem: A seasonal gift retailer's stateless web tier needs 20 instances all year and up to 120 during November and December. The application handles instance loss gracefully behind an ALB, and the company wants the lowest compute cost without risking the year-round baseline. Which combination of actions is the MOST cost-effective? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run the whole web tier, including the baseline, on Spot Instances only.
options.why: A large Spot reclaim could take out the baseline too, which the company does not want to risk.

options.text: Cover the 20-instance baseline with a Savings Plan.
options.why: The year-round baseline is certain, so a commitment gives the biggest discount on it.

options.text: Use an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy that adds Spot Instances across several instance types for the seasonal capacity above the baseline.
options.why: The stateless tier tolerates interruptions, so Spot covers the holiday peak at a deep discount, and diversification reduces interruptions.

options.text: Buy Reserved Instances for 120 instances to cover the peak.
options.why: Ten months of the year, 100 reserved instances would sit idle.

options.text: Run the holiday capacity on Dedicated Instances.
options.why: Dedicated Instances cost more than On-Demand and solve a different problem.

questions.explain: Layer purchases: commit (Savings Plans or RIs) for the steady baseline, On-Demand for unpredictable but critical extra capacity, and Spot for interruptible or stateless burst capacity.

questions.stem: A handmade-goods marketplace has its upload bucket in us-east-1. Sellers in Australia and Southeast Asia upload product videos of 1 to 4 GB directly from their browsers, and uploads are slow and often fail over long distances. Which solution will MOST improve upload speed with the LEAST change?

options.text: Create buckets in Sydney and Singapore and replicate them to us-east-1 with Cross-Region Replication.
options.why: It works, but the app must pick buckets per seller and manage several buckets, which is more change.

options.text: Put an Application Load Balancer and EC2 upload proxies in us-east-1.
options.why: Data still crosses the long-distance internet path before it reaches AWS, now with an extra hop.

options.text: Use AWS DataSync agents at each seller's location.
options.why: Sellers are many individuals using browsers; installing agents at their locations is not realistic.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and use multipart uploads.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration routes uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge over the AWS backbone, and multipart uploads retry only failed parts.

questions.explain: Long-distance uploads to one bucket: S3 Transfer Acceleration plus multipart upload. For downloads and caching, use CloudFront; for non-HTTP traffic, Global Accelerator.

questions.stem: A retailer replicates its product image bucket from eu-central-1 to eu-west-1 for disaster recovery. An audit requires that 99.9% of new objects reach the DR bucket within 15 minutes, with metrics and notifications when objects take longer. Which solution meets this requirement?

options.text: Turn on S3 Replication Time Control on the replication rule.
options.why: RTC is designed to replicate 99.9% of objects within 15 minutes, and it comes with replication metrics and late-replication notifications.

options.text: Keep standard Cross-Region Replication and add a CloudWatch alarm on bucket size in the destination.
options.why: Standard replication has no time SLA, and bucket size cannot show per-object delay.

options.text: Run a scheduled Lambda function every 15 minutes that copies new objects to the DR bucket.
options.why: Custom copying can miss objects, provides no SLA, and must be built and operated.

options.text: Use S3 Batch Replication every night.
options.why: Batch Replication is for existing objects or retries; nightly runs miss a 15-minute target.

questions.explain: S3 replication is asynchronous with no default time guarantee. When a stated replication SLA is required, add Replication Time Control, which also turns on the metrics needed to prove it.

questions.stem: A platform team at an e-commerce company wants product developers to create their own IAM roles for new Lambda functions without waiting for tickets. Security worries that a developer could create a role with more permissions than the developer has, for example AdministratorAccess. Which solution allows self-service while preventing this privilege escalation?

options.text: Have developers create roles through a shared IAM user whose access keys are stored in Secrets Manager.
options.why: A shared user hides who acted and still lets anyone attach any policy to the roles they create.

options.text: Let developers create roles only when they attach a specific permissions boundary, enforced with the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition key in their policy.
options.why: The boundary caps every role developers create, and the condition key rejects any role created without it.

options.text: Grant developers iam:CreateRole and iam:AttachRolePolicy, and review new roles weekly with IAM Access Analyzer.
options.why: A weekly review finds the escalation after it has happened instead of preventing it.

options.text: Attach an SCP to the developers' account that denies iam:CreateRole.
options.why: This prevents escalation by removing self-service altogether, which defeats the goal.

questions.explain: Permissions boundaries are the tool for delegating IAM administration safely: developers may create roles, but only roles that carry the boundary, so they can never grant more than the boundary allows.
